metadata.title: Are schools becoming more unequal? Insights from exploratory data mining of international large-scale assessment, TIMSS 2003-2019

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS science scale scores for Grade 4 and Grade 8 across five cycles (2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019) and computes school-level statistics from student-level plausible values. To obtain nationally representative school averages and variance components, the authors explicitly state that they used total student weight when computing PV-based weighted means (via intsvy). The paper does not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty estimation at the replicate level is not documented. Because the analysis is exploratory and focuses on variance decomposition and distributional modeling rather than supervised ML prediction, the weighting is used for descriptive/aggregation accuracy rather than as an ML training feature.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper describes PV generation and averaging across five PVs for each student and then aggregation to school-level statistics, but it does not document any explicit missing-data strategy (e.g., listwise deletion, imputation, or PV-specific missingness handling). This is a reporting gap because TIMSS microdata typically include some missing background or response information, and the variance/inequality decomposition could be sensitive to how missingness is treated. The authors also do not provide a missing-data flow or exclusion rule beyond filtering schools with fewer than 10 tested students.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to 10 countries that have complete TIMSS science data for all five cycles (2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019) at both Grade 4 and Grade 8. The study uses general science scores (not separate physics/biology/chemistry) to ensure comparability across systems. Schools are filtered to include only those with at least 10 students tested, yielding 7474 schools at Grade 4 and 7567 schools at Grade 8. For inequality decomposition, the authors compute school-level weighted averages from five PVs and then derive between-school and within-school variance components; they note that most schools contribute only one or two classes, limiting within-school decomposition beyond school-level variance.

main_findings.target_variable: Between-school vs within-school inequality (SD of science PV scale scores)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (descriptive inequality patterns; Between:Within ratio computed but no numeric values provided in the text).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 4 General Science the study leveraged country system, early tracking system, and grade level to characterize between-school and within-school achievement inequality, finding that between-school inequality is generally small relative to within-school inequality and that there is no clear worsening of between-school inequality over time. This indicates that policies aiming to reduce science achievement inequality should prioritize within-school instructional differentiation and support for lower-achieving students rather than focusing only on between-school stratification.

main_findings.target_variable: Between-school vs within-school inequality (SD of science PV scale scores)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (descriptive inequality patterns; Between:Within ratio computed but no numeric values provided in the text).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 8 General Science the study leveraged country system, early tracking system, and grade level to characterize between-school and within-school achievement inequality, finding that within-school inequality remains the dominant contributor to total inequality and that between-school inequality does not show a consistent upward trend. This indicates that even in systems with early tracking, reducing science inequality likely requires interventions that address heterogeneity within schools (e.g., differentiated instruction and targeted teacher support) rather than relying on tracking to homogenize outcomes.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 4 General Science (5 cycles; school-level aggregation)
main_findings.target_variable: Within-school inequality nature (SD vs within-school average; bimodality via Gaussian mixtures)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (directional results: moderate-to-large negative relationship between within-school SD and within-school average; bimodality indicated by multiple Gaussian components; Pearson’s r used but no numeric r values provided in the text).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 4 General Science the study leveraged country system, early tracking system, and grade level to relate within-school average achievement to within-school inequality, finding a consistent moderate-to-large negative relationship where higher-achieving schools are more internally equal and lower-achieving schools show substantially higher inequality. This indicates that school-level improvement strategies that raise average achievement may simultaneously reduce within-school dispersion, and that lower-achieving schools may need differentiated instructional approaches tailored to distinct student subpopulations rather than only remediating long lower tails.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 8 General Science (5 cycles; school-level aggregation)
main_findings.target_variable: Within-school inequality nature (SD vs within-school average; bimodality via Gaussian mixtures)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (directional results: negative relationship between within-school SD and within-school average; bimodality via Gaussian mixtures less established than Grade 4; no numeric correlations provided).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2003-2019 Grade 8 General Science the study leveraged country system, early tracking system, and grade level to examine within-school inequality patterns, finding that the negative association between within-school average achievement and within-school inequality persists across cycles and that lower-achieving schools are more likely to exhibit multiple subpopulations (Gaussian peaks). This indicates that inequality-reduction efforts should target within-school heterogeneity at the secondary level as well, and that tracking alone may not eliminate internal achievement dispersion.

data.outcome_summary: This exploratory data-mining study uses TIMSS science achievement data from 10 countries across five cycles (2003, 2007, 2011, 2015, 2019) for Grade 4 and Grade 8 general science. The authors compute school-level achievement using five plausible values (PV-based weighted means) and then decompose total achievement inequality into between-school and within-school variance components, filtering out schools with fewer than 10 tested students (7474 schools at Grade 4; 7567 at Grade 8). They report that within-school inequality is consistently much larger than between-school inequality and that between-school inequality does not show a clear worsening over nearly two decades. They further find a stable moderate-to-large negative relationship between within-school average achievement and within-school inequality, and they use Gaussian mixture modeling to show that lower-achieving schools often display bimodality (multiple student subpopulations), especially in Grade 4. Limitations include the lack of explicit missing-data handling documentation and the absence of numeric ML performance metrics because the work is descriptive/exploratory rather than supervised prediction.
